clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic B4GALNT1 variants; the gene encodes the enzyme (GM2/GD2 synthase) that adds N-acetylgalactosamine during complex ganglioside biosynthesis.
SPG26 is therefore a disorder of ganglioside metabolism - distinctive among the HSPs and conceptually linked to inborn errors of glycosphingolipid synthesis.
The typical picture is childhood- to early-adult-onset spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability or cognitive decline, dysarthria and a peripheral (axonal) neuropathy.
Extrapyramidal features such as dystonia and parkinsonism, together with cerebellar signs, frequently complicate the phenotype.
MRI often shows cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and cognitive and psychiatric features may progress over time.
Cataracts have been described, adding to the multisystem nature of the disorder.
A combination of pyramidal, extrapyramidal, cognitive and neuropathic features in a consanguineous pedigree should prompt B4GALNT1 testing.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG26 results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in B4GALNT1, which encodes beta-1,4-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase 1 (GM2/GD2 synthase). This enzyme catalyses a committed step in the synthesis of complex gangliosides such as GM2, GM1, GD2 and GD1a from simpler precursors. Deficient enzyme activity shifts the glycosphingolipid profile towards simple gangliosides and depletes the complex species that are critical for neuronal membrane signalling, myelin stability and axon-glia interaction. The resulting disturbance of ganglioside homeostasis produces a diffuse, length-dependent central and peripheral neurodegeneration, which explains the corticospinal (spastic), cerebellar, extrapyramidal, cognitive and peripheral-nerve components of the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (spastizin) - recessive complicated HSPs with cognitive impairment and a thin corpus callosum
SPG7 (paraplegin) - recessive HSP with cerebellar, optic and neuropathic features
Other metabolic/complicated recessive subtypes such as SPG35 (FA2H), SPG28 and SPG54
SPG23 (DSTYK) - recessive complicated HSP with pigmentary features (sibling subtype)
GM1 and GM2 gangliosidoses and other glycosphingolipid storage disorders
Autosomal recessive spastic ataxias including ARSACS, and neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation
additionalInvestigations: HSP gene panel or exome sequencing including B4GALNT1, with copy-number analysis
MRI of the brain to assess cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and white-matter change
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to define the axonal neuropathy
Ophthalmological review for cataract and other ocular signs
Metabolic work-up for glycosphingolipid disorders where a storage disease is considered
redFlags: Rapidly progressive cognitive or psychiatric deterioration requiring exclusion of a treatable or acquired encephalopathy
New extrapyramidal crises or marked dystonia needing symptomatic management
Visual failure or florid ocular signs beyond simple cataract
reference.prognosis: Progressive multisystem course; loss of ambulation and cognitive decline accrue over years, with disability driven by the combined pyramidal, extrapyramidal and cognitive burden.
pitfalls: Classifying SPG26 as a pure HSP and missing its multisystem (cognitive, extrapyramidal, neuropathic) nature
Overlooking the ganglioside-synthesis basis and its relationship to glycosphingolipid disorders
Attributing the extrapyramidal features to an unrelated movement disorder
Failing to screen for cataract and psychiatric involvement
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical review and classification
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; treat spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin, adding intrathecal baclofen for refractory tone
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and rehabilitation to preserve mobility
Treat the extrapyramidal features with dopaminergic therapy for parkinsonism and anticholinergic agents or botulinum toxin for dystonia
Speech and language therapy for dysarthria, with neuropsychological and psychiatric support for cognitive decline and behavioural change
Ophthalmological review with cataract surgery where visually significant, and podiatry for the axonal neuropathy
Genetic counselling with cascade B4GALNT1 testing for autosomal recessive inheritance
Escalate to multidisciplinary neurology as the combined pyramidal, extrapyramidal and cognitive burden accrues
